title: Larry's Birthday

jokes.text: Staff member sings 'Happy Birthday, Mr. President' to Larry in a Marilyn Monroe style, then awkwardly asks if he should just say 'Larry'
jokes.setup: Someone begins a grandiose Marilyn Monroe-style 'Happy Birthday, Mr. President' for Larry's birthday
jokes.punchline: He breaks the bit mid-song to ask 'Should I say Larry?' — instantly deflating the theatrical gesture
jokes.explanation: The Marilyn Monroe reference is instantly recognizable, and the deflation of breaking the bit to check in for approval is a good cringe opener. The joke is on the sycophantic culture around Larry — someone performing grandiosity but unsure it's welcome. Solid cold-open energy.

dialogue.speaker: Unknown singer
dialogue.line: ♪ Happy birthday, Mr. President ♪

dialogue.speaker: Unknown singer
dialogue.line: Mr. President? Should I say 'Larry'?

jokes.text: 'Has anyone else done this idea yet?' / 'Only Jojo in the commissary.'
jokes.setup: The staff member asks if anyone else has had the 'Mr. President' birthday idea as if it were an original creative concept
jokes.punchline: Yes — only Jojo in the commissary — a total nobody, making the grand tribute feel thoroughly unoriginal and small
jokes.explanation: Extremely economical. The name 'Jojo in the commissary' does a lot of work — anonymous, unglamorous, utterly deflating. The idea that a catering worker beat you to the 'brilliant' idea perfectly punctures the self-seriousness of celebrity birthday culture at a TV show. Good industry-insider texture.

dialogue.speaker: Unknown singer
dialogue.line: Has anyone else done this idea yet?

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Only jojo in the commissary.

jokes.text: 'What were you doing with that video camera a little earlier?' / 'Uh, the insurance people wanted a visual inventory of the office property.'
jokes.setup: Larry catches someone with a video camera and asks what they were doing with it
jokes.punchline: The obviously fabricated excuse — 'visual inventory of office property' — is transparently a cover for surprise birthday party prep
jokes.explanation: A functional bit — the 'insurance inventory' excuse is hilariously thin and Larry's 'Uh-huh' sell the fact that he's not buying it but also doesn't want to know. Competent sitcom setup for the birthday party premise.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Easy.

jokes.text: Larry's extended negotiation about NOT wanting birthday attention — 'I really don't want to do—' / 'Nobody's even thinking about your birthday, Larry.'
jokes.setup: Larry protests loudly and at length that he doesn't want any birthday fuss, covering every angle (no special gestures, no cards)
jokes.punchline: Beverly's deadpan 'Nobody's even thinking about your birthday, Larry' — the ultimate deflation, even though we just saw an entire room planning something
jokes.explanation: This is peak Larry Sanders characterization: his neurotic, narcissistic need to pre-negotiate every social situation while simultaneously craving the very attention he's rejecting. Beverly's punchline lands because it's the cruelest possible true/false response. The 'And let's not even open the cards this year' / 'Have there been many? Have they been coming in?' escalation within the negotiation is especially sharp — catching Larry mid-protest asking for validation anyway. Deserves a high character integration score.

dialogue.line: Uh, the insurance people wanted a visual inventory of the office property.

jokes.text: Larry: 'And let's not even open the cards this year.' / [Beat] 'Fine. Have there been many? Have they been coming in?'
jokes.setup: Larry instructs Beverly not to make a big deal of the birthday, specifically not to open cards
jokes.punchline: Immediately pivots to 'Have there been many? Have they been coming in?' — revealing his desperate need to know anyway
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The whiplash between 'don't open the cards' and the immediate 'have there been many?' in the same breath is a masterclass in character-driven comedy. It's a perfect X-ray of Larry's soul: he wants not to care but cannot survive not knowing. The trailing 'Ok. Never mind' as he catches himself is the cherry. Structure is impeccable — setup, beat, reversal, self-correction. Could only be Larry Sanders. Comparable to 8.0 anchor quality.

dialogue.line: Nobody's even thinking about your birthday, Larry.

jokes.text: Hank to Larry: 'What is your real age anyway? And while you're at it, why don't you give me your real weight? Make it saucy.'
jokes.setup: Hank is wishing Larry a happy birthday in an obsequious way
jokes.punchline: Pivots to jabbing at Larry's vanity about age and weight, then adds 'Make it saucy' — a bizarre non-sequitur that's pure Hank
jokes.explanation: 'Make it saucy' is a perfect Hank Kingsley non-sequitur — pompous, slightly off, delivered with complete sincerity. The jab about age and weight in the middle of birthday praise is classic Hank: he means well but can't help undermining. Good character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: For a 55-year-old guy, you look a little heavy.
Ouch.

jokes.text: Larry: 'You sounded almost sincere.' / Hank: 'Well, you can't fake feelings like that.'
jokes.setup: Hank has just delivered a rambling, obviously insincere birthday toast
jokes.punchline: Hank insists 'you can't fake feelings like that' — in complete sincerity, with no awareness of the irony
jokes.explanation: The deadpan irony of 'you can't fake feelings like that' delivered about something so obviously faked is sharp. Hank's total lack of self-awareness is the engine. The exchange is economical and perfectly captures the show's sensibility: performative sincerity mistaken for the real thing.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: You sounded almost sincere.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Well, you can't fake feelings like that.

jokes.text: Artie on Mike Patterson: 'He spent the whole time kissing Joel Grey's ass.'
jokes.setup: The writers are debating the new hire Mike Patterson and his credentials
jokes.punchline: Artie's damning character indictment — not about his writing ability, but that he spent the Tonys kissing Joel Grey's ass
jokes.explanation: Very Larry Sanders — the insider showbiz reference (Joel Grey at the Tonys) used as a character assassination tool. Artie's moral compass is always about who a person is, not what they can do. The specificity of Joel Grey makes it funnier than a generic name would.

dialogue.line: That wasn't bad. It sucked, man.

jokes.text: Artie on practical jokes in the writers room: 'Sure, you know, the old thumbtack on the chair, peanut butter in the wallet, whatever the fuck you guys are always giggling about in there.'
jokes.setup: Someone mentions Mike Patterson is 'a fun guy to have in the room'
jokes.punchline: Artie lists juvenile practical jokes with complete disdain, ending with 'whatever the fuck you guys are always giggling about in there' — dismissing the entire writers room culture
jokes.explanation: Pure Artie. The specificity of 'peanut butter in the wallet' as a practical joke example is absurd and perfect. The contemptuous 'whatever the fuck you guys are giggling about in there' is a wonderful dismissal of the entire notion of fun. It's also a meta-joke: the showrunner/producer who finds his own show's writers room childish. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: He spent the whole time kissing Joel Grey's ass.

jokes.text: Artie's reveal that Mike is arriving in half an hour, after Phil has been arguing for 'dialogue' and consensus
jokes.setup: Phil makes a speech about how glad he is that they're all 'dialoguing' about whether Mike is the right thing to do
jokes.punchline: Artie: 'Well, I'm so glad you're glad because Mike will be here in half an hour.' The decision was already made — the dialogue was theater.
jokes.explanation: Excellent structure. Artie lets Phil go through the whole 'I'm glad we had this dialogue' performance, and then drops the reveal that it was never a dialogue at all. It's a perfect encapsulation of TV production power dynamics — management invites 'input' after the decision is finalized. The timing is impeccable. Strong Artie character moment.

dialogue.line: What finally convinced him, the quality of our riots?

jokes.text: Writers' paranoia about options: 'My option's up in a month... When's your option up?' / 'In a week.' / 'Right there.'
jokes.setup: Phil and Jerry are discussing Mike Patterson's arrival and its implications
jokes.punchline: The conversation quickly reduces to each man calculating how long until they're fired — 'In a week.' / 'Right there.' — delivered with quiet dread
jokes.explanation: Dark and economical. 'In a week.' / 'Right there.' is the whole joke — the laconic acknowledgment that one of them is about to lose their job, delivered with the same tone as noting the weather. Shows the industry paranoia Larry Sanders excels at.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: As usual, I'd like to see more of that humor on the page.

jokes.text: Hank barging in to make sure no one is giving Larry the same present: 'A Shetland pony?'
jokes.setup: Hank knocks and asks if anyone is giving Larry the same present he is
jokes.punchline: Someone deadpans 'A Shetland pony?' — an absurd non-answer that mocks the premise of Hank's anxiety
jokes.explanation: 'A Shetland pony?' is a perfectly calibrated absurdist response — it's specific enough to be funny (not just 'a horse'), absurd enough to derail Hank, and delivered deadpan. The writers clearly enjoy messing with Hank. Sharp one-liner.

dialogue.speaker: Phil
dialogue.line: A shetland pony?

jokes.text: The gold bracelet that 'looks like something Sammy Davis Jr. would have worn'
jokes.setup: Hank reveals his birthday gift — a gold bracelet he loves so much he'd buy it for himself
jokes.punchline: Someone notes it 'looks like something Sammy Davis Jr. would have worn' — with Hank accepting 'Oh, thanks' as if it's a compliment
jokes.explanation: The Sammy Davis Jr. reference is dead-on — it implies gaudy, Rat Pack-era excess, perfect for the bracelet Hank would love. The real joke is Hank's 'Oh, thanks' taking it as a compliment. Very character-specific to Hank's oblivious grandiosity.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: It looks like something Sammy Davis Jr. would have worn.

jokes.text: The Mickey Mantle autographed baseball gift vs. Hank's bracelet — 'You win... Larry loves baseball.'
jokes.setup: Hank is proudly showing off his expensive gold bracelet gift for Larry
jokes.punchline: Someone reveals they're getting Larry a 1957 Mickey Mantle autographed baseball — Hank immediately concedes 'You win' with a theatrical sigh
jokes.explanation: Hank's instant concession 'You win' — not 'that's lovely' or 'Larry will love both' — is perfect. It reveals that gift-giving for Hank is a competitive sport. Has rewatch value because it sets up the Mike Patterson baseball callback at the end.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: I thought we were going to get him gag gifts this year.

jokes.text: Hank: 'I thought we were going to get him gag gifts this year.'
jokes.setup: Hank has just learned his bracelet is outclassed by the Mickey Mantle baseball
jokes.punchline: He retroactively claims the plan was gag gifts — transparently revising history to save face
jokes.explanation: Hank's immediate face-saving lie is brilliantly Hank. The fact that he just spent multiple lines praising the bracelet makes the pivot funnier. This is the kind of real-time self-deception that makes Hank such a rich character.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: I bought Larry plastic vomit.

jokes.text: Hank: 'I thought we were going to get him gag gifts this year.' Long pause. 'Do you guys know any other baseball players Larry really, really likes?'
jokes.setup: Hank has just conceded defeat in the gift competition ('You win')
jokes.punchline: He immediately pivots to trying to compete again with another autographed baseball — the 'I thought we were doing gag gifts' is a transparent face-saving lie, and 'any OTHER baseball players' is the tell
jokes.explanation: The 'gag gifts' excuse followed immediately by 'any other baseball players' is perfect sustained character comedy — Hank's self-deception is complete and unselfconscious. 'Did you guys hear me? Well, get back to me on it.' as he's ignored is an excellent button. Very strong Hank characterization.

dialogue.speaker: Mike
dialogue.line: I'm pretty sure I parked in Nitro's space. He'll probably just pick the car up and move it.

jokes.text: Jerry: 'Fuck. I bought Larry plastic vomit.'
jokes.setup: Jerry has heard that someone is giving a brilliant, thoughtful Mickey Mantle baseball
jokes.punchline: Reveals his own gift — plastic vomit — in a flat moment of defeated self-awareness
jokes.explanation: Perfectly timed and delivered. 'Fuck. I bought Larry plastic vomit.' is three words of setup and three words of punchline — maximum economy. The gag gift premise Hank floated moments ago is now revealed to be true for Jerry, who's genuinely distressed about it. Pays off the gag gift thread with precision.

dialogue.speaker: Phil
dialogue.line: I'm sure one will be opening up very soon.

jokes.text: 'Only if it comes from the heart.'
jokes.setup: Jerry asks if he should get Larry something really good after realizing plastic vomit is inadequate
jokes.punchline: 'Only if it comes from the heart' — sincere-sounding advice about gift-giving when they're all clearly in panicked competition mode
jokes.explanation: A mild ironic jab — the show-business sincerity advice landing hollow. Functional filler, not a standout.

dialogue.speaker: Phil
dialogue.line: Larry could hardly even look at me. It wasn't my imagination?

jokes.text: Mike Patterson's first concern: parking near the American Gladiators set — 'I'm pretty sure I parked in Nitro's space.'
jokes.setup: Mike is being introduced to the writers room on his first day at the show
jokes.punchline: His first priority is anxiety about parking in 'Nitro's space' — a specific, absurd Hollywood adjacency joke
jokes.explanation: The American Gladiators parking space is a perfect piece of early-90s Hollywood geography comedy. 'He'll probably just pick the car up and move it' as the punchline nails it — both a joke about Gladiator performers and about L.A. parking anxiety on day one at a new job. Good insider texture.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Louis XIII is much more than cognac... After four sips, he fell asleep at the Christmas party. Exactly. That's what Larry likes to do.

jokes.text: Jerry on a parking spot opening up: 'I'm sure one will be opening up very soon.'
jokes.setup: Mike asks if there are any parking spots available
jokes.punchline: Jerry says one will open soon — implying that when one of them gets fired, their spot is available. Dark and delivered without affect.
jokes.explanation: Devastatingly economical dark comedy. In one throwaway line, Jerry reveals that he knows he or Phil is about to be fired to make room for Mike, and he delivers it as bland hospitality information. The gap between the dark implication and the casual delivery is the whole joke. Near-perfect economy.

dialogue.speaker: Delivery guy
dialogue.line: Including a $5.00 rush delivery, it's $32.12...

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: There's been a mistake. I ordered Louis XIII.

jokes.text: Phil and Jerry panicking about Mike: 'Larry could hardly even look at me.' / 'I know, I saw it.' / 'It wasn't my imagination?' / 'I don't think so.' / 'Oh, shit!'
jokes.setup: Mike has just been introduced to the staff for the first time
jokes.punchline: Phil and Jerry immediately enter full existential panic mode, micro-analyzing every eye movement Larry made for signs of impending termination
jokes.explanation: The recursive anxiety loop — 'It wasn't my imagination?' / 'I don't think so' — is true to the paranoid culture of TV writing rooms and is quietly hilarious. The escalating affirmation between two equally scared people is a good cringe engine.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: It's like hot piss.

jokes.text: Artie on firing a writer: 'Just want to throw them all in the cage together and see who survives?'
jokes.setup: Larry asks if they can 'wait a while and see how they all work out together' before deciding who to fire
jokes.punchline: Artie's paraphrase: 'Just want to throw them all in the cage together and see who survives?' — delivered with the weary clarity of someone who's seen this before
jokes.explanation: Artie's translation of Larry's HR-speak into brutal honesty is exemplary. The cage metaphor is both funny and accurate — this is exactly what TV show producers do. Artie's weary acceptance ('Uh, that would be up to you') makes it darker. Strong Artie character integration.

dialogue.line: They gave Julio Gallo a very nice funeral. The only problem was when it was time to close the casket, nobody could find the cork.

jokes.text: Artie on Louis XIII cognac: 'After four sips, he fell asleep at the Christmas party.' / 'Exactly. That's what Larry likes to do.'
jokes.setup: Beverly challenges Artie on why he gives Larry the same bottle of cognac every year
jokes.punchline: When Beverly points out Larry fell asleep after four sips, Artie affirms: 'Exactly. That's what Larry likes to do.' — revealing this is a feature, not a bug
jokes.explanation: A genuinely great Larry Sanders joke. Artie's gift philosophy — get Larry something that puts him to sleep — is both the best articulation of their relationship and a beautiful dark joke about what Larry 'likes.' The structure is clean: Beverly presents it as a criticism, Artie flips it into endorsement. 'That's what Larry likes to do' as a definitive statement of someone's soul is both affectionate and devastating. Comparable in quality to the 8.0 anchor.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: You have fucked at least three interns that I know about, one right out there behind the fucking desk.

jokes.text: The cognac order mix-up: Artie ordered Louis XIII, received Grand Orsage — 'Grand Orsage? Larry doesn't drink that shit. It's like hot piss.'
jokes.setup: The delivery arrives and the cost is only $32 — Artie realizes something is wrong
jokes.punchline: 'Grand Orsage? Larry doesn't drink that shit. It's like hot piss.' — Artie's outrage and the vivid descriptor
jokes.explanation: 'Hot piss' as cognac criticism is a great phrase. Artie's absolutism about Larry's tastes is both funny and touching. The farce of the wrong bottle arriving creates good physical comedy energy even in a dialogue-only scene.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: You have to be a genius to get away with that kind of stuff. You're not getting away with it, jer.

jokes.text: Artie's wine joke about 'Julio Gallo': 'They gave Julio Gallo a very nice funeral. The only problem was when it was time to close the casket, nobody could find the cork.'
jokes.setup: Artie is outraged about the cheap wine substitution and starts reciting a joke to the delivery person about Julio Gallo
jokes.punchline: 'Nobody could find the cork' — the casket/cork pun on the wine baron's name
jokes.explanation: A deliberately corny joke-within-a-joke — Artie telling a wine snob's groan-worthy pun. The joke works mostly because of the character context: Artie directing a funeral pun at a delivery person who mixed up his cognac order. The pun itself is old-school and thin but has a certain period charm.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Don't sweat it, kiddo. It's a good deal. You're getting fired. They have to pay you for a month.

jokes.text: Response to Artie's Julio Gallo joke: 'The eulogy was subtle but fruity?' / 'No, that's bad.'
jokes.setup: Artie has just told the Julio Gallo funeral/cork joke
jokes.punchline: Someone tries an alternative punchline — 'The eulogy was subtle but fruity' — and Artie immediately dismisses it: 'No, that's bad.'
jokes.explanation: The meta-comedy of a writers room workshopping a bad joke and the head writer immediately killing the alternative is very Larry Sanders. 'The eulogy was subtle but fruity' is actually a decent wine pun, which makes Artie's flat 'No, that's bad' even funnier — it's also a comment on Artie's taste. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: I just fell in love with this beauty, so I treated myself because I deserve it.

jokes.text: Artie's list of Jerry's professional misconduct: 'You come in late, take naps, pick girls out of the audience lineup for their numbers, and have fucked at least three interns — one right out there behind the fucking desk.'
jokes.setup: Artie is explaining to Jerry why he's being let go
jokes.punchline: The list escalates from 'comes in late' to 'fucked at least three interns — one right out there behind the fucking desk' — ending with the specific geography of the desk
jokes.explanation: A great escalating list joke. The escalation from professional to personal to flagrantly sexual is well-paced, but the specific payoff — 'one right out there behind the fucking desk' — is what makes it exceptional. The physical specificity ('right out there') makes it vivid and real. Then Artie punctuates with 'You have to be a genius to get away with that kind of stuff' — a devastatingly backhanded judgment. Strong character integration (only Artie can deliver this with moral authority and black humor simultaneously).

dialogue.line: The network owns the company that makes those. The cost to them is nothing.

jokes.text: 'You have to be a genius to get away with that kind of stuff. So — you're not getting away with it, jer.'
jokes.setup: Artie has just listed all of Jerry's misconduct
jokes.punchline: The pause before 'So—' followed by the devastatingly gentle 'you're not getting away with it, jer.' The 'jer' especially — tender even as he's firing him.
jokes.explanation: The best pure joke delivery in the episode. The setup is that a genius could get away with all that behavior — establishing a criterion. The 'So—' beat creates anticipatory silence. 'You're not getting away with it, jer.' is the twist: not 'you're fired' but 'you're not a genius.' The diminutive 'jer' kills it — Artie likes this kid even as he terminates him. This is Rip Torn at his best. Structure is near-perfect, economy is exceptional, character integration is total. Justifies 8+ scoring.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: He said, 'Clint, do you know Hank?' And do you know what that simple gesture did? It just made my day.

jokes.text: Jerry's dawning realization: 'Oh my god, it's me.' / Artie: 'That's right.' / 'Don't sweat it, kiddo. It's a good deal. You're getting fired. They have to pay you for a month.'
jokes.setup: After Artie's budget speech, Jerry suddenly realizes he's the one being fired
jokes.punchline: Artie consoles him: 'Don't sweat it. It's a good deal. You're getting fired. They have to pay you for a month.' — presenting termination as a financial opportunity
jokes.explanation: Artie's pragmatic silver lining — 'It's a good deal. You're getting fired. They have to pay you for a month' — is a wonderful piece of industry cynicism. Presented not as cruelty but as genuine helpful advice from someone who's been around. The flat matter-of-factness is the whole joke.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Some guy offered to blow me for three bucks. What'd you do? I gave the guy three bucks. He looked like he could use it.

jokes.text: Hank wearing the bracelet he bought 'for Larry': 'Oh thanks. You like it? Is that supposed to be for Larry?' / 'No, no, no. I just fell in love with this beauty, so I treated myself because I deserve it.'
jokes.setup: Someone compliments Hank's bracelet, which he was supposedly buying for Larry
jokes.punchline: Hank has already appropriated it for himself — 'I treated myself because I deserve it' — and claims he got Larry 'the perfect gift'
jokes.explanation: Exceptional payoff. Hank bought a gift for Larry, decided he liked it too much, kept it, and now has to pretend he always had a different gift. 'I deserve it' as justification is peak Hank Kingsley — no guilt, pure entitlement. Also perfectly sets up that Hank will have nothing to give Larry at the party. Rewatch bonus because this plants a flag that pays off later.

dialogue.line: But what did he do, jerry?

jokes.text: The exercise bike from the network: 'The network owns the company that makes those. The cost to them is nothing.'
jokes.setup: Someone laments that the network sent Larry an exercise bike as a birthday gift
jokes.punchline: The reveal that the network owns the manufacturer — so it cost them nothing — reframing corporate largesse as pure self-interest
jokes.explanation: A tidy industry satire joke about corporate gift-giving as self-promotion. The specificity ('the cost to them is nothing') is what makes it land — it's not just cynical, it's accurate. Good Larry Sanders texture.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Ok, so I'm a little slow, all right? But what I'm saying is, have you made the video yet?

jokes.text: 'Who wants to go to the Smokehouse and get fucking hammered?' / 'All right, I'm in. Larry's birthday, right?' / 'Larry coming?' / 'Oh, no, no, no.'
jokes.setup: Jerry has just been fired; his response is to organize a group drinking expedition
jokes.punchline: The instant clarification that Larry is NOT invited to his own birthday celebration — the fired writer is appropriating the birthday as his own occasion for drinking
jokes.explanation: Good dark character beat — Jerry dealing with being fired by treating Larry's birthday as his personal excuse to get drunk. The 'Larry coming? Oh no no no' is funny because it's both logical (Larry would kill the vibe) and petty (it's his birthday).

dialogue.speaker: Sugar Ray Leonard
dialogue.line: Don't get me angry.

jokes.text: Hank's concern about his lighting: 'I'm worried that the one spotlight makes me look insane.'
jokes.setup: Hank is preparing to record his birthday tribute video for Larry
jokes.punchline: 'I'm worried the one spotlight makes me look insane' — a vanity concern perfectly aligned with Hank's self-image issues
jokes.explanation: Character-specific vanity moment. 'Look insane' rather than 'look bad' is the right word choice — Hank has a particular fear of appearing unhinged that tracks with the character. Functional but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: This conversation is not unlike what it must be to fight you, 'cause you feel like... You're surprising me, and I'm not that-- I'm doing the best I can.

jokes.text: Hank's birthday tribute: The Clint Eastwood story — 'He sits down, doesn't shake my hand... You know what Larry did? He said, 'Clint, do you know Hank?' And do you know what that simple gesture did? It just made my day.'
jokes.setup: Hank is recording a heartfelt video birthday tribute to Larry, recounting a meaningful night
jokes.punchline: The entire significant memory is about Clint Eastwood being introduced to Hank by Larry — that's it. The big emotional story is 'Larry said my name to a famous person,' which Hank treats as a profound gift.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best moments. The mismatch between the grandiosity of Hank's setup and the smallness of the actual memory is devastating character comedy. 'Clint, do you know Hank?' as the pivotal gesture that 'made his day' says everything about Hank's status anxiety and his psychological dependence on Larry's validation. It's funny AND sad AND true. The fact that he cries doing it makes it richer. Pure Hank Kingsley — no other character on television could deliver this.

dialogue.line: Those are sissy shoes.

jokes.text: Hank's tribute take fails because he said 'big star' instead of 'big, big star' — insisting they reshoot it
jokes.setup: Hank has just delivered a seemingly sincere birthday tribute video
jokes.punchline: The retake argument is over whether he said 'big star' or 'big, big star' — the doubling of 'big' being apparently crucial to Hank's intended tribute
jokes.explanation: The perfect coda to the tribute scene. The emotional moment is immediately undercut by Hank's insistence on a retake for a trivial word choice. 'Big star' vs. 'big, big star' is the kind of thing only Hank would care about — it reveals that even his most 'sincere' moments are performances he's directing. Wonderful character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Knock that shit off, you guys.
Sorry, Artie.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Listen, I picked that fucking goddamn tie out myself.

jokes.text: Jerry's Denny's birthday sketch pitch: 'Larry walks into a Denny's for a birthday meal.' [Chuckles] 'Boy, that sounds good, jer.'
jokes.setup: Jerry, who has just been fired, pitches a birthday bit where Larry goes to Denny's
jokes.punchline: The response 'Boy, that sounds good, jer' is clearly patronizing — the idea is not good, and everyone knows Jerry is fired, making the polite encouragement darkly funny
jokes.explanation: The pathos of a fired writer pitching jokes to colleagues who now have to be polite to him is quietly funny. The 'boy that sounds good jer' is a perfect non-encouragement encouragement. The Denny's idea is bad enough to be funny in itself for a prime-time talk show host.

dialogue.speaker: Party guests
dialogue.line: Surprise!

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Beverly, didn't I ask you--

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: I know. But I surprised you, didn't I?

jokes.text: Jerry at Wendell's at 4am: 'Some guy offered to blow me for three bucks.' / 'What'd you do?' / 'I gave the guy three bucks. He looked like he could use it.' / 'But what did he do, Jerry?'
jokes.setup: Jerry casually mentions he was at a diner at 4am when a man offered him oral sex for three dollars
jokes.punchline: He gave the man the money — but the punchline is withheld by Jerry not completing the story, and the writer's follow-up 'But what did he do, Jerry?' goes unanswered
jokes.explanation: Exceptional dark comedy. The joke operates on multiple levels: (1) the deflation of 'I gave him the money' as purely charitable — the most unexpected response, (2) the withheld final punchline of whether the man performed, and (3) the framing that Jerry, who has just been fired, was eating alone at a diner at 4am when this happened — painting a portrait of a man in free fall. 'He looked like he could use it' is a great line. The follow-up 'But what did he do, Jerry?' going unanswered is the final beat — the show refuses to resolve it. Near 8.0 anchor quality.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: This is $1,100 a bottle. $75 a shot. And this is the last bottle in the western U.S.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: You're goddamn right it is.

jokes.text: Jerry still working after being fired: 'Didn't you, like, leave the show yesterday?' / 'Yeah, you know, everyone gets weird, ok? Everything's cool.'
jokes.setup: Phil discovers Jerry is still at his desk the day after being fired
jokes.punchline: Jerry's nonchalant 'everyone gets weird, ok? Everything's cool' — refusing to acknowledge the reality of his situation
jokes.explanation: A perfect piece of denial comedy. 'Everyone gets weird' as an explanation for why a person has been terminated is a beautifully unhinged rationalization. The breezy 'Everything's cool' while he sits at his old desk doing old work is pure cringe-comedy gold.

dialogue.speaker: Darlene
dialogue.line: Because I know that you love-- gadgets. Math.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I love math. And gadgets. Math and gadgets.

jokes.text: Phil gently escorting Jerry out: 'Hey man, will you come outside with me? Wanna work outside?' / 'Yeah bring all your stuff.' / 'You sure?' / 'Yeah.'
jokes.setup: Phil realizes Jerry isn't leaving voluntarily and has to somehow get him out
jokes.punchline: He invites Jerry to 'work outside' — a gentle fiction that doesn't acknowledge the reality of the situation, and Jerry goes along with it
jokes.explanation: The social delicacy of 'Wanna work outside?' as a way to remove a fired employee without confrontation is a great cringe beat. Both men are participating in a polite fiction. 'You sure? Yeah.' as the final confirmation before Jerry grabs his stuff is sad and funny simultaneously — proto-Office energy.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Oh, I feel like Levar Burton in Roots: The Next Generation.

jokes.text: Staffers debating birthday gifts for Larry: 'A book about dogs. What the fuck? I heard he likes dogs.' / 'Where the fuck did you hear that?' / 'I read it somewhere.'
jokes.setup: Two crew members are comparing what they're getting Larry for his birthday
jokes.punchline: One has gotten a book about dogs based on a magazine item — the other is stunned — 'Where the fuck did you hear that?' — highlighting the absurdity of celebrity gift research
jokes.explanation: A background gag about the culture of staff gift-giving — reading celebrity profiles to figure out what to give the boss. 'Where the fuck did you hear that?' is a good line. Minor but amusing texture.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Yeah, Artie and I both pitched in on the cognac.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: No, uh-- So you both pitched in?

jokes.text: Larry's on-air interview with Sugar Ray Leonard becoming a running confusion loop about whether the music video is out, done, or neither
jokes.setup: Larry interviews Sugar Ray Leonard, who is apparently also releasing a music video
jokes.punchline: Larry becomes hopelessly confused about whether the video is 'done' vs. 'out' — the interview devolves into recursive clarification attempts that Sugar Ray escalates with 'Don't get me angry'
jokes.explanation: A brilliant piece of talk-show satire. The interview circles the same confusion multiple times — is it done? Is it out? What's the difference? — because Larry can't let go of a point he doesn't understand. 'Don't get me angry' from Sugar Ray Leonard playing himself is wonderful — a boxing champion threatening a talk show host over interview questions. Larry's 'Ok, so I'm a little slow, all right' is a great self-deprecating beat. The bit escalates naturally and has good cringe energy.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Uh, yeah, Larry, I hope I made it clear that the cognac is from both Arthur and myself.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: So you both pitched in?

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: No, uh--

jokes.text: 'This conversation is not unlike what it must be to fight you, 'cause you feel like you're surprising me, and I'm not that — I'm doing the best I can.'
jokes.setup: Larry is repeatedly confounded by Sugar Ray Leonard during the interview
jokes.punchline: Larry compares the confusion of the conversation to being physically hit by a boxer — acknowledging that he's being beaten in both arenas simultaneously
jokes.explanation: A clever self-aware interview joke. Larry comparing the experience of being confused by Sugar Ray to being physically fought by him is both apt and flattering to the guest. It's the kind of quick-wit pivot a great interviewer makes — except here it's also genuinely true, which makes it funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: That's my gift to Larry.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Hey, thanks.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Could you blow out the candles?

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: The cake is heavy.

jokes.text: Larry to Sugar Ray mid-interview: 'Those are sissy shoes.'
jokes.setup: The interview is stumbling; someone (Hank?) makes an aside about Sugar Ray's shoes
jokes.punchline: 'Those are sissy shoes' — an absurd, childish insult injected mid-celebrity interview, presumably muttered off-mic
jokes.explanation: The absurdist non-sequitur quality of this — interrupting a professional boxing champion interview to critique his footwear — is the joke. Brief and economical.

dialogue.speaker: Francine
dialogue.line: Oh, my god. Who threw up? What is that?

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: That's my gift to Larry.

jokes.text: Artie through the earpiece: 'Knock that shit off, you guys.' / Larry: 'Sorry, Artie. Listen, I picked that fucking goddamn tie out myself. Which one of you guys has got a problem with that? That's what I thought.'
jokes.setup: During the live interview, someone mocks Larry's tie on air
jokes.punchline: Artie interrupts through the earpiece, and Larry uses the authority of Artie's voice to shut down the mockery — then claims personal ownership of the tie choice
jokes.explanation: The earpiece-as-authority-extension is a great Larry Sanders device. Artie functioning as Larry's off-screen muscle during the interview, and Larry pivoting his embarrassment into wounded pride ('I picked that fucking tie out myself') is perfect host vanity comedy. The 'That's what I thought' to no response is a nice deadpan button.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Well, fuck you, ok? Because a, I know I've been fired. And b, if you think I wanna celebrate that fact with you fucks, you're out of your fucking mind.

jokes.text: Sugar Ray Leonard Nintendo game confusion: 'Have you made that yet?' / [Laughing] 'Hello.'
jokes.setup: Larry asks about Sugar Ray's Nintendo game the same way he asked about the video — whether it's 'been made' yet
jokes.punchline: 'Have you made that yet?' again — Sugar Ray's 'Hello.' as a comedically small response to a returning confusion
jokes.explanation: The callback to the video confusion lands because it's the same mistake in a new context — Larry literally hasn't learned. 'Hello.' is a perfect minimalist response — Sugar Ray can't even believe it's happening again. Good running gag payoff.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Larry, is this your little way of letting me know that I've been fired? Well, fuck you, ok? Because a, I know I've been fired. Artie told me. And b, if you think I wanna celebrate that fact with you fucks, you're out of your fucking mind, ok?

jokes.text: Artie's phone call rage mid-episode: 'Cognac! Booze! Hooch! Huh? Oh, go fuck yourself.'
jokes.setup: Artie is still trying to resolve the wrong cognac delivery during the broadcast
jokes.punchline: His escalating synonyms — 'Cognac! Booze! Hooch!' trying to communicate with someone on the phone — end with the inevitable 'Go fuck yourself'
jokes.explanation: The escalating synonyms — 'Cognac! Booze! Hooch!' — is a great frustrated-phone-call bit. 'Go fuck yourself' as the final capitulation is perfect Artie. The joke works because we've seen this cognac thread building all episode, and Artie's volcanic but precise profanity is always satisfying.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: This is the best party I've ever had.

jokes.text: The surprise birthday party — Beverly: 'But I surprised you, didn't I?' / Larry: 'Oh my god. You did. You totally surprised me.'
jokes.setup: Despite Larry's explicit instructions at the start of the episode not to do anything for his birthday, a surprise party has been organized
jokes.punchline: Larry's theatrical shock: 'Oh my god. You did. You totally surprised me. Oh, you guys.' — a complete performance of surprise from a man who knew something was coming
jokes.explanation: The payoff to the entire episode's setup — Larry said he didn't want a party, the party happened anyway, and Larry performs the expected delight. It's a small ironic payoff — Larry secretly wanted this — but it's earned. The callback to his opening neurosis is satisfying.

dialogue.speaker: Phil
dialogue.line: I was gonna give him a Mickey Mantle one! I got it in the car! I already got him a Mickey Mantle one!

jokes.text: The surprise party: 'Surprise!' Larry: 'Beverly, didn't I ask you—' / 'I know.' / 'But I surprised you, didn't I?' / 'Oh my god, you did. You totally surprised me.'
jokes.setup: Larry explicitly asked Beverly NOT to plan anything; she did anyway
jokes.punchline: Beverly's logic — that the surprise element justifies the betrayal — and Larry's immediate capitulation ('You totally surprised me') is perfect: his whole speech about not wanting this collapses the second it's actually executed
jokes.explanation: This pays off the entire episode's opening setup. Larry's very specific, emphatic demand that Beverly not plan anything is immediately undermined by his genuine delight at being surprised. 'You totally surprised me' delivered with actual warmth by someone who spent the first act demanding no surprises is a perfect character reveal: he wanted it all along. Strong structure, excellent callback payoff.

dialogue.speaker: Phil
dialogue.line: I was gonna give him a Mickey Mantle one! I got it in the car! I already got him a Mickey Mantle one!

jokes.text: The Louis XIII reveal — it's $1,100 a bottle, $75 a shot, 'the last bottle in the western U.S.' — and Hank immediately claims he chipped in on it.
jokes.setup: Larry opens Artie's cognac gift and everyone oohs over it
jokes.punchline: Hank, who bought a gold bracelet and kept it for himself, immediately announces the cognac is from both him and Artie — 'I just wanted to make that clear'
jokes.explanation: Perfect Hank character payoff across the whole episode. He bought a gift, kept it, and now is piggybacking on Artie's $1,100 bottle of cognac as if he contributed. 'I just wanted to make that clear' is the perfect self-incriminating button — his desperation to be seen as generous while being demonstrably selfish is pure Hank Kingsley. Strong rewatch bonus as the culmination of a long thread.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: I remember right before I gave up stand-up, I was at Catch a Rising Star, and I was bombing horribly. And there was one guy in the back that was laughing, and it was you.

jokes.text: Darlene's gift — a calculator — and Larry's response: 'Because I know that you love... gadgets.' / 'Math.' / 'I love math.' / 'And gadgets. Math and gadgets.'
jokes.setup: Darlene gives Larry a calculator and tries to explain her gift choice
jokes.punchline: The stumbling back-and-forth — 'gadgets'... 'math'... 'I love math'... 'math and gadgets' — is a small cringe exchange about a bad gift being graciously received
jokes.explanation: A small cringe beat — the social discomfort of receiving an obviously thoughtless gift and both parties fumbling to justify it. 'I love math' as Larry's save is a mild laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Happy birthday, asshole.

jokes.text: The VR headset: 'Oh, I feel like LeVar Burton in Roots: The Next Generation.'
jokes.setup: Someone gives Larry a virtual reality headset at the party
jokes.punchline: Larry puts it on and says 'I feel like LeVar Burton in Roots: The Next Generation' — combining the VR headset visual with a celebrity lookalike joke and a TV show title mixup
jokes.explanation: A tight early-90s pop culture joke. LeVar Burton wore the VISOR device in Star Trek: TNG, but Larry conflates it with Roots — mixing up two of Burton's most iconic roles in one absurd image. The joke works on multiple levels: the VR goggles visual, the celebrity reference, and Larry's characteristic slight misfiring on the pop culture detail. Good economy.

jokes.text: Larry receives a calculator from Darlene: 'Because I know that you love— gadgets. Math. I love math. And gadgets. Math and gadgets.'
jokes.setup: Darlene gives Larry a calculator for his birthday
jokes.punchline: Larry struggles to find anything positive to say about a calculator as a birthday gift, eventually landing on 'math and gadgets' as two separate enthusiasms he apparently has
jokes.explanation: A good cringe beat. Larry's polite struggle with a calculator gift — trying to manufacture enthusiasm for 'math' — is relatable social discomfort elevated by his status as a TV host. Darlene's proud 'gadgets' explanation is sweetly misguided.

jokes.text: Hank's second attempt to claim credit for the cognac: 'Yeah, Artie and I both pitched in on the cognac. I just wanna make that real clear.'
jokes.setup: Hank has already once claimed to have co-gifted the cognac
jokes.punchline: He says it again — 'I just wanna make that real clear' — the repetition revealing how important this false credit is to him
jokes.explanation: The callback to the cognac credit grab. The repetition — 'I just wanna make that real clear' said twice — is the joke. Hank's compulsive need to re-stake his claim in the same party reveals a deep insecurity. Each repetition is funnier than the last.

jokes.text: Francine arrives, and the plastic vomit is revealed as someone's gift — 'Oh my god. Who threw up? What is that?' / 'That's my gift to Larry.'
jokes.setup: Francine arrives at the party and sees what appears to be vomit on the table
jokes.punchline: 'That's my gift to Larry' — confirming the plastic vomit gag gift, paid off from the earlier Jerry scene
jokes.explanation: Good payoff to the plastic vomit setup from earlier. Francine's genuine alarm ('Oh my god, who threw up?') followed by the deadpan 'that's my gift to Larry' is a classic visual gag callback. The joke was planted well enough that the payoff satisfies.

jokes.text: Jerry's birthday party eruption: 'And b, if you think I wanna celebrate that fact with you fucks, you're out of your fucking mind, ok? Get the fuck outta here! Because I have just enough integrity left to get the hell outta here... So you can just take your little cake and you can shove it right up your fucking ass! Put it in your ear!'
jokes.setup: Jerry appears at Larry's surprise birthday party after being fired
jokes.punchline: Jerry delivers a full meltdown speech ending with 'shove it right up your fucking ass — put it in your ear!' — the correction of anatomical location being the comic button on an explosion
jokes.explanation: The episode's biggest comedic moment. The speech is a brilliantly structured escalation: righteous anger, self-awareness ('I know I've been fired'), wounded dignity ('just enough integrity left'), and then the spectacular descent into 'shove it up your ass — PUT IT IN YOUR EAR' — the anatomical correction being the perfect absurdist button. 'Put it in your ear' as a self-correction after 'shove it up your ass' is genuinely inspired. The rage is earned, the delivery is comic gold, and it's character-specific to Jerry's particular flavor of wounded pride.

jokes.text: Larry: 'This is the best party I've ever had.' (immediately after Jerry's meltdown)
jokes.setup: Jerry has just erupted in a profane tirade at Larry's birthday party
jokes.punchline: Larry's breezy 'This is the best party I've ever had' — either genuine or deeply ironic, delivered without affect
jokes.explanation: Perfect. Five words that land like a gut punch. After Jerry's explosive meltdown — the plastic vomit, the chaos — Larry's 'This is the best party I've ever had' is simultaneously: (1) ironic relief, (2) a character revelation (Larry likes controlled chaos that isn't about him), (3) maximally economical. The understatement is devastating. This line will be in highlight reels. Maximum economy score — not a single word wasted.

jokes.text: Jerry's post-meltdown calm: 'I feel very calm, all right? I'm letting go. I feel, uh... I feel at peace for the first time in my life. I'd like to kiss you, man.'
jokes.setup: After his explosive meltdown, Jerry now returns claiming to be 'at peace'
jokes.punchline: 'I feel at peace for the first time in my life. I'd like to kiss you, man.' — the catharsis of public humiliation experienced as spiritual liberation, climaxing with a desire to kiss Larry
jokes.explanation: The whiplash from 'put it in your ear' to 'I feel at peace for the first time in my life' is hilarious — the catharsis is genuine but absurd. 'I'd like to kiss you, man' as a resolution to a furious confrontation with your boss/the man who fired you is perfectly unexpected. Good escalation-to-absurdism arc.

jokes.text: Artie: 'I'm watching you, Jerry.' — repeated twice as Jerry tries to hug people
jokes.setup: Jerry has swung from explosive to suddenly peaceful and affectionate
jokes.punchline: Artie continues to watch him like a hawk even as Jerry expresses peaceful intentions — 'I'm watching you, man'
jokes.explanation: A good Artie beat — his distrust of Jerry's sudden calm is warranted and funny. The repetition of 'I'm watching you' while Jerry becomes increasingly cuddly is an amusing contrast. Solid character comedy but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Mike Patterson gives Larry a Hank Aaron baseball — 'I got you a baseball. It's autographed by Hank Aaron right there.' — triggering chaos over the Mickey Mantle one
jokes.setup: The Mickey Mantle autographed baseball has been the episode's gold standard gift
jokes.punchline: Mike Patterson — the new guy — has independently brought a Hank Aaron signed baseball, setting off a chaotic dispute with Phil who has the Mantle ball in the car
jokes.explanation: The episode's most structurally elegant callback. The Mickey Mantle baseball has been the standard against which all gifts are measured — and the new writer, trying to endear himself, brings the exact same category of gift, sabotaging Phil's punchline gift. The fact that it's Hank Aaron vs. Mickey Mantle (both legends, but different) makes it precise rather than redundant. The resulting chaos — Darlene crying, people clamoring — is a perfect escalation button. Very well-engineered across the episode arc.

jokes.text: Darlene starts crying after the baseball confrontation. 'Someone scared Darlene.' 'Darlene, please.' 'She got upset.'
jokes.setup: The party has descended into chaos — Jerry's meltdown, the baseball dispute
jokes.punchline: Darlene's disproportionate emotional response to the mild chaos; the way the party continues awkwardly around her distress
jokes.explanation: Mild party chaos beat. Darlene's fragility adds to the general disorder but isn't a strong joke in itself. Functional texture.

jokes.text: Hank's birthday tribute video (final version): 'Oh, big star. And Clint comes out. He sits down. Doesn't shake my hand. Oh, no.' — now with 'big, big star' corrected, delivered to camera in formal surroundings
jokes.setup: We see the final version of Hank's birthday tribute video — the one he insisted on reshooting because he said 'big star' instead of 'big, big star'
jokes.punchline: The story is identical, the 'big, big star' is now there, but Hank's emphasis on this trivial change makes the whole production feel even more absurd
jokes.explanation: The payoff to the 'big, big star' retake argument. Hearing the corrected version — and realizing the correction makes zero meaningful difference — validates that Hank's perfectionism was entirely about ego management. The callback enriches the original scene enormously on rewatch.

jokes.text: Unknown tribute writer: 'I remember right before I gave up stand-up, I was at Catch a Rising Star and I was bombing horribly. And there was one guy in the back that was laughing — and it was you.'
jokes.setup: A writer is delivering a video birthday tribute to Larry
jokes.punchline: The tribute is that Larry was the only person laughing when this writer was bombing in a comedy club — and Larry told him to give up stand-up and take up writing. Intended as heartwarming, it's actually a low-key roast: Larry was the one who ended this guy's stand-up career.
jokes.explanation: A genuinely poignant and funny moment. The writer means this as a tribute, but it's also the story of Larry watching someone bomb and suggesting they quit. 'I don't know. It was cool. I won't forget it. I'm glad you were born' as the close is perfectly awkward — a tribute that inadvertently reveals Larry as the man who killed someone's dreams with a compliment. The show's insider showbiz sensibility at its best.

jokes.text: Larry, watching Jerry leave through the parking lot window: 'I'm better than this. I gotta talk to him.' Artie: 'Let him make a clean break.'
jokes.setup: Jerry is making his exit from the parking lot; Artie says to let him go
jokes.punchline: Larry's 'I'm better than this' — claiming a moral high ground before immediately running after Jerry — the irony being that chasing a fired employee in a parking lot is NOT being better than this
jokes.explanation: Good Larry characterization — the self-aggrandizement immediately preceding an undignified action. The show earns this through consistent character work.

jokes.text: 'Happy birthday, asshole.' [Rock thuds]
jokes.setup: Larry approaches Jerry in the parking lot after everything — the firing, the meltdown, the peace
jokes.punchline: 'Happy birthday, asshole.' followed by the thud of a rock hitting glass
jokes.explanation: The episode's best joke. After everything — the birthday neurosis, the surprise party, Jerry's explosion and spiritual awakening — Larry tries to connect with Jerry in the parking lot, and receives a rock through his window and 'Happy birthday, asshole.' The phrase does triple duty: (1) it IS a birthday greeting, technically, (2) 'asshole' is Jerry's honest final verdict on Larry, and (3) the rock thud is the perfect punctuation. Economy is perfect — five words plus a sound effect close out an entire storyline. The callback to the entire episode's tension makes this emotionally and comedically satisfying. This is what a 9+ looks like in this show's register.

jokes.text: Larry's 43rd birthday video wish: '...here's to 43 great more years. You take care of yourself.' [Happy Birthday plays]
jokes.setup: A birthday video tribute wishing Larry many more years
jokes.punchline: 'Here's to 43 great more years' — wishing a man 43 more years of life as if he's turning 43, after a whole episode where his real age has been a source of anxiety
jokes.explanation: A mild ironic button — the number of years wished onto Larry (43) echoes his age anxiety from earlier. Functional closer, not a standout joke on its own.

tmdb_overview: Larry celebrates his birthday and the gang all struggle to top each other with their birthday gifts to him. Meanwhile the celebration is darkened by the firing of one of the writers.
